title: Soreng district explained: Sikkim's newest district
meta_description: Soreng, carved from West Sikkim in December 2021: where it is, how to get there from NJP and Bagdogra, what is where, permits and how long to spend.
summary: Soreng became Sikkim's sixth district in December 2021, carved from West Sikkim. It covers the south-western hills between Jorethang and the Nepal border, including Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Okhrey, Hilley and the Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary. It is about 100 km and 4–6 hours from Siliguri. Indians need no special permit.

sections.heading: A new district on an old map
paras: In December 2021 Sikkim went from four districts to six under the Sikkim (Re-organisation of Districts) Act, 2021. Pakyong was carved out of East Sikkim, and Soreng out of West Sikkim, which was renamed Gyalshing district. The other two were renamed too: North Sikkim became Mangan district and South Sikkim became Namchi district. Soreng town became the headquarters of the new district.

The change is still catching up with the world. Many maps, booking sites, bus boards and even some signboards still say West Sikkim for Rinchenpong, Kaluk or Okhrey, and travellers search for them that way. If you see Rinchenpong, West Sikkim, it is the same place. On this site we use both names where it helps.

Soreng is small. The district administration gives its area as roughly 17,600 hectares and its population at about 65,000 in the 2011 census. It borders Nepal to the west along the Singalila ridge, Gyalshing district to the north, Namchi district to the east and the Darjeeling hills of West Bengal to the south.

sections.heading: What is where
paras: Think of the district as three bands. In the north, the Rinchenpong and Kaluk ridge faces Kangchenjunga and has most of the hotels and resorts. In the middle are Soreng bazaar, the headquarters, and farming villages around Daramdin and Mangalbarey, which is the second subdivision. In the west the road climbs through Sombaria to Okhrey and Hilley, the gateway to the Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary on the Nepal border.

Most villages lie between about 500 m and 2,600 m, according to the district administration, while the sanctuary's ridges rise above 4,000 m. That spread means oranges and cardamom in the warm valleys and rhododendron and oak forest higher up.

sections.heading: Getting there
paras: There are no flights or trains into Soreng. Pakyong airport has had no scheduled flights since June 2024, and the Sevoke–Rangpo railway is not yet open, so plan on Bagdogra airport (IXB) or New Jalpaiguri station (NJP). The district administration puts Soreng about 125 km from Bagdogra, 115 km from NJP and 100 km from Siliguri.

The road follows the Teesta on NH10 to Melli, the check post where you enter Sikkim, then turns up the Rangeet valley to Jorethang. The bridge over the Rangeet at Jorethang is the main way into Soreng district from Namchi district. From Jorethang, roads climb to Soreng, Rinchenpong and Kaluk, and through Sombaria to Okhrey and Hilley. NH10 closes after landslides in the monsoon; the alternative is to come via Darjeeling down to Jorethang, which adds one to two hours. Check current status before you travel.

Shared jeeps run from Siliguri to Jorethang and from Jorethang to Soreng, Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Daramdin and Sombaria. The Sikkim Nationalised Transport also runs buses on some routes. For Okhrey and Hilley, a reserved car for the last stretch is usually needed.

sections.heading: Who lives here
paras: Soreng is one of the most mixed corners of a mixed state. The 2011 census figures for the area now forming the district, summarised on Wikipedia, show Nepali as the most common mother tongue, followed by Limbu at about 14 percent, then Lepcha, Sherpa and Tamang. About 40 percent of people belong to Scheduled Tribes. Roughly half are Hindu, a little over a quarter Buddhist and about one in eight Christian, and most villages have a temple, a gompa and a church within walking distance of each other.

Place-names carry this history. The Soreng district website explains Daramdin as coming from the Lepcha word dalom, a place of rest or flat land, which fits its broad farmland. It also records a local story, as told locally, of villagers who tried to build a tower of clay pots to reach the sky until a misheard word brought it down.

sections.heading: Permits and fees
paras: Indian travellers need no special permit for any part of Soreng district that visitors normally go to. Like everywhere in Sikkim, a ₹50 per tourist entry fee is collected by your hotel or homestay at check-in, valid for 30 days, and children under five are exempt. The Barsey sanctuary charges a separate forest entry fee at Hilley, roughly ₹50 a day for Indians.

Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit to enter the state. Since 12 January 2026 there are no paper permits: apply online on the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India, with approval in about 24–48 hours. Soreng district has no further protected-area permit requirement for the usual visitor areas. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Seasons and money in brief
paras: Soreng has two peak seasons. The first runs from mid-March to the end of April, when the Barsey rhododendrons flower and Okhrey and Hilley are at their busiest; the peak bloom on the Hilley to Barsey trail is usually from the last week of March to the last week of April. The second runs from October to December, with the clearest views of Kangchenjunga from Rinchenpong and Kaluk, dry trails and cool, sunny days. January and February are cold and quiet, with snow possible at Hilley. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain, leeches and road closures, and few visitors.

The district is one of the cheapest parts of Sikkim to visit. Family homestays charge about ₹1,200–2,200 per person a night including meals, small hotels about ₹1,500–3,000 a room, and village resorts in Kaluk and Rinchenpong from about ₹3,000 a room. A shared jeep seat from Siliguri to Jorethang costs about ₹250–350, and a reserved small car from NJP to Rinchenpong about ₹4,500–6,000. There are no entry tickets for the monasteries and viewpoints, only the Barsey forest fee. Our budget guide to Soreng sets out sample costs line by line. All figures are indicative for 2026; check current status before you travel.

Mobile signal is good in Soreng bazaar, Jorethang and most of the Rinchenpong and Kaluk ridge, and patchy around Okhrey, Hilley and inside the sanctuary. Carry cash for a few days, as small villages may have no working ATM.

sections.heading: How long to spend and how to combine it
paras: Two nights is the minimum for Soreng, because the drive in takes most of a day. Three to four nights lets you split time between the Rinchenpong and Kaluk ridge and Okhrey for the Barsey walk. Soreng combines naturally with Pelling, about 1.5–2 hours from Rinchenpong, and with Yuksom beyond it. It also links east to Namchi and Ravangla in Namchi district via Jorethang, which makes a good loop for travellers going on to Gangtok. If you have only a weekend, stay on the Rinchenpong and Kaluk ridge; if you are coming in April, give Okhrey priority.

3 nights: Okhrey with the Barsey walk, ideally in April
5–6 nights: add Pelling, or Namchi and Ravangla

faqs.a: Soreng district was created in December 2021 under the Sikkim (Re-organisation of Districts) Act, 2021, carved out of what was then West Sikkim. It became Sikkim's sixth district, alongside Pakyong, which was carved from East Sikkim at the same time. Soreng town is the headquarters. Many maps and booking sites still list its villages under West Sikkim.

faqs.q: Is Rinchenpong in West Sikkim or Soreng?
faqs.a: Rinchenpong is now in Soreng district. Until December 2021 it was part of West Sikkim, which has since been renamed Gyalshing district, and many maps, booking sites and travel blogs still describe it as West Sikkim. It is the same place either way. Kaluk, Okhrey, Hilley and the Barsey sanctuary also moved to Soreng district.

faqs.q: How do I reach Soreng from NJP or Bagdogra?
faqs.a: By road only. From NJP or Bagdogra the route follows NH10 to Melli, then the Rangeet valley to Jorethang, and climbs into Soreng district. Rinchenpong is about 125 km and 5–6 hours from NJP by car. Shared jeeps run Siliguri–Jorethang and on into the district. In the monsoon NH10 can close; the alternative is via Darjeeling.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Soreng?
faqs.a: Indians need no special permit, only the ₹50 Sikkim tourist entry fee collected at check-in and the forest fee for Barsey. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online on the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India; there are no paper permits since 12 January 2026. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is Soreng district famous for?
faqs.a: It is best known for the Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary, which flowers from March to May, and for the Rinchenpong and Kaluk ridge, with wide views of the Kangchenjunga range and an 18th-century monastery. It also has Sherpa and Limbu village life, homestays, orange and cardamom farms, and far fewer visitors than Pelling or Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is the headquarters of Soreng district?
faqs.a: Soreng town, a hill bazaar at roughly 1,300 m, is the headquarters. It has the district offices, a few small hotels such as The Orchid Hotel, and shared jeep links to Jorethang. Most visitors pass through rather than stay, basing themselves in Rinchenpong, Kaluk or Okhrey, which have better views and more homestays.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Soreng?
faqs.a: At least two nights, because getting there from NJP takes most of a day. Three to four nights is better: two in Rinchenpong or Kaluk and two in Okhrey for the Barsey walk. With five to seven nights you can add Pelling and Yuksom, or Namchi and Ravangla, for a fuller loop of western and southern Sikkim.

faqs.q: Is Soreng good for first-time visitors to Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want quiet villages and mountain views more than shopping and big sights. The altitude is moderate, roads are decent, and Indians need no permits. First-timers often combine two nights in Rinchenpong or Kaluk with Pelling. If you want snow, lakes and high passes, add Gangtok and North Sikkim on a longer trip.

faqs.q: Which is the nearest railway station to Soreng?
faqs.a: New Jalpaiguri (NJP) in West Bengal is the nearest major railway station, about 115 km from Soreng bazaar and roughly 5–6 hours by road from Rinchenpong or Okhrey. Bagdogra (IXB) is the nearest airport, about 125 km away. The Sevoke–Rangpo railway into Sikkim is not open yet; completion is targeted for December 2027.
